reviews.text: I always loved Nevergrind's minimalistic approach. It's like if you take an MMO and strip it down to its core mechanics. I've spent 120 hours in Nevergrind Online and I'd gladly do it again if there only was still an active playerbase. Now this game is tailored to be a single player experience and it's perfect for just hopping in and grinding away. The combat feels very engaging and much faster paced due to the combo mechanic. As soon as my class started to take off after a couple of levels, I found myself glued to the screen.

I played the browser game a lot and really glad the game was remastered and put on steam! Very unique ARPG where you control the action by pulling monsters. Tons of classes all with very different playstyles. The new UI and turbo mode are amazing! [Random Gameplay] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TA0DqZgpDOE

This is a chill game that can be played with just your hand on the mouse, which after a draining day at work, is the perfect way to spend some time gaming, without having to get too involved. If you played EverQuest, you will definitely recognize class descriptions and sound effects too. The dopamine inducing "DING!" of a level up will forever be a sound that warms my heart. I have played up to defeating the first boss, so far. In the game you will create a character with options of races and classes, a character portrait and then you will begin to run through the game's quest. It's essentially small bits of narrative text that gets you to your next area where you are fighting monsters, getting loot and leveling up. That is the game's core loop. It is a combat and character progression game. The story is there to pull you along, but the meat and potatoes is the combat. Combat is real time, not turn based. The "Chain Combo" system is a press your luck style mechanic. You pull a monster, begin combat, and then you can pull in more. So long as at least one mob is still alive when you pull, you will increase your combo, yielding more XP, gold, and the chance to find items. Balancing your ability timers will be how you get through it. I can see myself putting a good amount of time in this. The accessibility plus character progression focused gameplay is a really nice mix for me. Not sure about it? Check out the demo.

For everyone that doesn't know (everyone by the looks of it), this was a free to play browser RPG that has been on the internet for i dont even know how long. I found it about 11 years ago and played it heavily for like a year. With the developer porting the game to steam he completely annihilated it off the internet and now you can only find old forum posts about it. The game is genuinely great for what it is, the game is really fast paced compared to any other game like this ive played. This version is so good that I actually was very disappointed with nevergrind online when i saw how slow paced it was. Nevergrind being removed from browsers is a huge stain on this developers legacy. before he had the greatest browser rpg ive ever played, rivaling adventurequest even. Here on steam he will be lucky to get 1000 reviews and the game will surely be buried into obscurity and forgotten about. The developer deserves money for the work he put into this game, but to delete your legacy in order to make like a thousand bucks is absolutely insane work.

The game is interesting, in a way. It hits that part of your brain that gives quick dopamine hits every time you get a gear drop or level up. Unfortunately, for me, it's killed by: [list] [*] [b]Complete lack of QoL:[/b] no auto sort, no way to sort at all, no search in the bank, no way to auto summon monsters to keep the combo counter going. Yeah, I know you can press 'D', but mashing it every second or two just to keep enemies at max count is something that should be automatable. It serves no gameplay purpose other than to punish you if you lose a 58k combo streak because you missed a keypress. [*] [b]Complete lack of information given to the player:[/b] tooltips, stats, skills and skill (active skills vs. passive weapon or spell school skills) are barely explained. [*] [b]Complete lack of UX[/b] for basic stuff like mouse clicks. Looking at you, bank transfers. At least we can one-click sell. [*] [b]Redundant mechanics:[/b] why have rare gear with randomized stats when uniques are just straight up better, and the combo bonus fills your inventory with uniques within 15 minutes of play? The merchant also feels pointless past the very early game. [*] [b]A ton of classes that don't really specialize.[/b] You get 12 talents, which mostly just represent the 12 skills a class has access to, but they cap at 20 each and 110 total, so you end up with what you actually use plus some leftovers. [/list] I know the game's an EverQuest 1 clone, so maybe the whole point is nostalgia. I never played EverQuest 1 though, so I can't judge it on that front. I also never played the original Nevergrind, the 2015 web game, but this version somehow feels like a rehash of that 2015 version. And what worked in 2015 doesn't necessarily work in 2026.

I give it a good review, but there are conditions: You must play this game using Autohotkey, utilizing Claude AI to maximize your character's skill casting logic. Without Autohotkey, you'll play like a "pianist"—it's a loot-hunting game, and your hands will definitely get crippled after a long time. The game's skill logic operates on a perfect casting loop; if you can't perfectly cast skills, you won't be able to unleash your character's true potential. This game "should have an auto-skill casting feature," and using Autohotkey was a decision made out of necessity.

It's basically a single player, combat-focused version of Everquest without the running around. It "borrows" sound effects, classes, races, ability names, etc directly from EQ, but simplifies & rebalances things to make it work for each class (maybe a bit oversimplified, actually). You can choose how many enemies you'd like to fight at a time, and when they appear, so you can customize your experience that way. Since you're encouraged to chain fight enemies, much of the challenge of the game is in managing your resources to fight as many as possible in a row. Would be better if you could control multiple party members in a turn based experience, but this is still rather enjoyable for what it is. Probably up to 6.5-7/10 depending on your EQ nostalgia level and class choice. Editing to say that now that I have a higher level character, combat is considerably more chaotic, yet fun. This game can be surprisingly addictive and I'm finding tons of unique gear for other characters. But if you're going to play for more than a couple hours, I *highly* recommend starting as a Druid, Necromancer, Magician, or Shaman to be able to handle large groups. Paladin & Shadowknight are too defensively oriented. Cleric & Enchanter don't kill fast enough. Rogue & Wizard don't stay alive well enough. Bard has slow casting songs that constantly get interrupted (and it's too easy to accidentally interrupt them yourself, too).

It's Everquest for tired old men with families and jobs. I played the original EQ for many years since it was released and still have incredibly fond memories of my time with it and have wished that I could capture some of that magic again. And since I no longer have the luxury of time to spend several weeks farming an off-hand stick that raises my int by 3 points, Nevergrind manages to capture a lot of the essence of EQ, or really MMO's in general, in a streamlined, efficient manner that old men who like seeing numbers go up will crave. That it is also unapologetically mimicing classic Everquest's class/race/skill/spell systems is just icing on the cake for oldheads looking to wistfully smile at nostalgia. Otherwise, it's just a solid, fun reduction of MMO's with an addicting Diablo-esque loot system and risk/reward of pulling more mobs to keep a combo going for increasing exp and items. Simple, addicting and it respects your time. You should give it a shot.
